newsitem.title: DUBAI: UAE firm still backs Pakistan oil refining project.
newsitem.headline: UAE firm still backs Pakistan oil refining project.

text.p: A subsidiary of Sharjah's Crescent Petroleum Co International Ltd is persuing an oil hydrocracker project in Karachi despite sharp differences with its proposed local partner, the firm said on Monday.

Pakistan's state-owned State Petroleum and Marketing Co (Perac) informed Crescent in July that it was unilateraly ending its 1993 agreement with Crescent Refining and Marketing Co to develop the hydrocracker.

Crescent is backing the plant which would have the capacity to convert 1.65 million tonnes a year (roughly 35,000 barrels per day) of fuel oil supplied from two local refineries into products, mostly high speed diesel.
The project's total cost, including finance, is $692 million.
"We are committed to the project with or without our partner Perac," a manager at Crescent in Sharjah said.
Crescent has taken legal advice on Perac's withdrawal.

Negotiations with the Pakistani government over the "implementation agreement" will resume shortly after British consultants Arthur Andersen provides the government this week with its final report on measures that Pakistan could adopt to attract foreign oil investment.
An initial Andersen report was presented to Islamabad in August which included an analysis of the project's internal rate of return.
Pakistan's petroleum policy offers foreign investors a 25 percent return on equity though firms say that the return is only guaranteed in rupees and not dollars.

Pakistan is reliant on refined oil product imports to meet growing industrial and agricultural demand and has opened its downstream sector to foreign investment to meet supply gaps and limit scare foreign currency expenditure.
The products from the proposed Crescent cracking plant would be sold in the local market.
Construction of the plant would take 33 months.
Sharjah is one of the seven emirates that make up the oil rich United Arab Emirates (UAE).
